title: Three-Week IB English Literature Revision Plan
summary: IB English Literature revision plan for November: triage texts, practise essays, complete timed papers, and protect your rest across three focused weeks.
body_markdown:
Three weeks is enough time to improve your preparation, but not enough to revise everything equally. A strong **IB English Literature revision plan** for November should identify gaps, turn literary knowledge into analysis, and build confidence through timed writing.


The aim is to arrive able to interpret unfamiliar writing, compare studied works, and organise an argument under pressure. Adjust these focused sessions around your official examination timetable, other subjects, and whether you take SL or HL.


### Your three-week overview


Week Main priority What you should produce


Week 1 Diagnose and triage Text maps, a Paper 1 baseline, and Paper 2 plans


Week 2 Build analytical fluency Timed paragraphs, comparative outlines, and corrected essays


Week 3 Simulate and taper Full timed papers, recall sheets, and protected rest


Prioritise active writing, compare authorial choices, and review feedback before attempting another response. Preserve time for other subjects and reduce your workload during the final 48 hours.


### Week 1: Diagnose before you revise


Familiarity can feel like progress. Yet revisiting a favourite novel may leave your main weaknesses untouched: thin knowledge of another work, weak comparison, or paragraphs that describe rather than analyse.


### Build a text triage map


For each potential Paper 2 work, make a one-page map covering:


- Three central concerns or tensions.
- Five flexible moments from the work.
- Recurring structural and stylistic choices.
- Narrative, dramatic, or poetic perspective.
- Connections with another work.


Mark areas green if you can explain them without notes, amber if your analysis needs development, and red if your knowledge is unreliable. Maintain green areas briefly, strengthen amber areas, and prioritise essential red areas.


RevisionDojo’s[English study resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-english-langlit-new) can support concept review, although this linked collection covers Language and Literature. Check its relevance to your Literature course. Use Flashcards to retrieve literary terms and textual details, then explain their significance aloud.


### Complete a Paper 1 baseline


Write about an unfamiliar literary passage under realistic conditions. At SL, practise selecting and analysing one passage; at HL, schedule practice reflecting your greater Paper 1 workload. Follow the current instructions and timing for your level.


Review whether your thesis offers a defensible interpretation, paragraphs analyse precise choices, and discussion explains effects rather than listing techniques.


The[IB English Literature Paper 1 Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader/rubric/english-literature-paper-1) offers another feedback source. Compare automated guidance with your teacher’s advice and official assessment criteria.


### Plan Paper 2 before writing it


Paper 2 requires a comparative response on two literary works to one of four questions. Practise adapting your knowledge by selecting four varied questions and allowing 10 minutes per plan. Produce a thesis, three comparative claims, and supporting moments from both works.


Use the[IB English Paper 2 structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/understanding-the-ib-english-a-literature-paper-2-exam-structure-or-language-and-literature-guide) to check that comparison drives your argument.


### Week 2: Build analytical fluency


Aim for five sessions of 45-60 minutes, a lighter review day, and a rest day. If another examination comes earlier, reduce English sessions rather than sacrificing sleep.


Rotate between these tasks:


- Write a Paper 1 thesis and two analytical paragraphs.
- Select a Paper 2 question and build a comparative plan.
- Repair your weakest Week 1 topic.
- Complete timed Paper 1 practice.
- Write a timed Paper 2 introduction and body section.


The[Paper 1 and Paper 2 study comparison](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-s-the-best-way-to-study-for-paper-1-vs-paper-2) helps distinguish close reading of unfamiliar literature from comparative discussion of studied works.


### Practise comparison within paragraphs


Begin with a shared claim answering the question. Analyse a precise choice in one work, connect or contrast it with the other, and explain why the relationship matters. This keeps both works in conversation throughout the argument.


Consult these[Paper 2 strategies for working under time pressure](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-prepare-for-the-ib-english-paper-2-exam-under-time-pressure-or-revisiondojo-strategies) if your structure slips. Ask RevisionDojo’s AI Chat to challenge a thesis or suggest counterarguments, then check every suggestion against the works.


### Turn feedback into a specific repair


After each task, record one weakness and one action. Replace “improve analysis” with “explain how narrative distance affects the reader’s judgement.” Practise that repair in your next paragraph. Grading tools can help identify patterns; Tutors can offer guidance when a problem persists.


A student negotiates with a crowned stack of books while another offers a pillow as a ceasefire


### Week 3: Simulate, then taper


Complete one full Paper 1 and one full Paper 2 early in the week, matching your level’s requirements. Use official specimen material, examination questions supplied through authorised channels, or RevisionDojo Predicted Papers and Mock Exams.


Use the[RevisionDojo Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/questionbank) for targeted practice and[Test Builder and Exam Mode](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/test-builder) for uninterrupted timed work. Test question selection, planning, pacing, and decision-making alongside your literary knowledge.


Review each simulation that day or the following morning. Choose no more than three priorities so your remaining sessions have a clear purpose.


### Protect the final 48 hours


Review text maps, plan one comparative response, and annotate a short unfamiliar extract. Rehearse timings, organise permitted materials, and decide when studying will stop.


Avoid a full paper late on the final evening. Fatigue can make one disappointing attempt seem more significant than it is. Rest supports the concentration and judgement that literary analysis requires.


### Fit English around your November timetable


On demanding days, use a 20-minute maintenance task: retrieve five textual moments, plan a thesis, or analyse a short passage. Save simulations for longer study blocks.


Leave completed coursework alone unless your school advises otherwise. The Coursework Library belongs primarily to drafting preparation; these weeks should focus on assessments still ahead.


Use RevisionDojo as your central resource for notes, retrieval, feedback, and examination practice. Let each session end with something concrete: a stronger paragraph, a clearer comparison, or a corrected misconception. Three focused weeks can make your response to the examination more deliberate.
